items.scene: Tia realizes she broke her promise to return a book on time. She apologizes and says it was her fault.
items.question: Which moral emotion is most supported?
items.why_this_case_matters: Self-blame for a norm violation points directly to guilt.

items.scene: Ben misses the train and worries he will be late to class. No one blames him.
items.question: Which moral emotion is most supported?
items.why_this_case_matters: The upset comes from an event outcome, not from blame, duty, or wrongdoing.

items.scene: Sara hides her smile during the award dinner because her family told her not to show excitement in public.
items.question: What is the main reason for her behavior?
items.why_this_case_matters: This is about masking emotion, not inferring a moral emotion.

items.scene: Owen gets irritated when the store closes early and ruins his plans. No one wronged him.
items.question: Which moral emotion is most supported?
items.why_this_case_matters: This targets the common shortcut of labeling any upset as anger, even without wrongdoing.
